heading: ‘Contemporary Now’: How Chennai is building a new art collector base | Mint
author: Anindo Sen
paragraphs: This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.

After its debut last year, a lot was expected from the second edition of Contemporary Now. The art event, organised by Ashvita, opened on 7 August in Chennai and is expected to go on till 25 August. The galleries from the inaugural edition—Chatterjee & Lal, Ashvita’s, Chemould Prescott Road, Experimenter and Vadehra Art Gallery—have been joined by Project 88 and TARQ this time.

Being held across two floors of the recently renovated Lalit Kala Akademi, the expanded edition features 162 artworks by 66 artists from India and abroad. It is significant to note that women visual art practitioners account for nearly half the lineup, and the average age of the participating artists is 47. “The numbers show that it often takes more than two decades for an artist to find recognition at the highest level. You could be 45 years old and still be considered emerging,” shares Ashvin Rajagopalan, founder of Ashvita’s Gallery and Contemporary Now. Some of the featured artists include Anju Dodiya, Jitish Kallat, Jagannath Panda, Reena Saini Kallat, Mithu Sen, LN Tallur, Atul Dodiya Pushpakanthan Pakkiyarajah, Jasmine Nilani Joseph and Radhika Khimji, besides collectives and institutions like the RAQS Media Collective and Chanakya School.

The works are priced between ₹1 lakh to ₹72 Lakhs with 84% of the works available for a little under ₹15 lakhs, which suggests a relatively accessible entry point for works by leading contemporary artists. This has also been made possible in part by the curatorial choice of including a large selection of works on paper.

“I wanted to show the best of contemporary art from the country in Chennai. These are works, which might have been shown at art fairs and galleries in Delhi and Mumbai, but have not been accessible physically to our clients in the city until now,” shares Priyanjoli Basu, director, Contemporary Now. A recent Knight Frank Report indicates that Chennai accounted for 4.8% of Ultra High Net Worth Individuals (UHNWIs) in the country in 2025, up from 1.3% in 2015, suggesting a latent appetite for art which can be tapped into.

Jaiveer Johal, Chennai-based entrepreneur and art collector, has been in regular attendance, often guiding local visitors, who might be relatively new to the idea of collecting contemporary art. “When I started collecting, I learnt a lot from the gallerists. However, conversations between collectors were missing,” he elaborates. “What I like about Contemporary Now is the organisers recognise that the market will follow the conversation, not the other way round.”

Beyond the main venue of Lalit Kala Akademi, galleries in the city are hosting parallel exhibitions as well. Ashvita’s, for instance, has hosted solo shows by Benitha Perciyal K and by C Krishnaswamy at its two galleries in Mylapore, while Gallery Veda in Nungambakkam has organised a group show on the theme of Madras Abstraction. Johal has curated ‘I have a Dream’, an introspective studio exhibition at the home of Chennai-based artist George K, covering decades-long practice after he transitioned from a merchant banker to an artist.

Given the response this year, Mortimer Chatterjee and Tara Lal of Chatterjee & Lal are optimistic about the future of Contemporary Now. “We represented three artists associated with the recent edition of the Kochi Biennale—curator Nikhil Chopra, Minam Apang and Nityan Unnikrishnan. We were thrilled by the number of people who recognised the works of these artists having visited the Biennale,” they say. “This is exactly the kind of sustained engagement with specific practices which often leads to converting an interested art enthusiast into a committed collector.”

Brendan Embser, senior editor at Aperture, a publishing imprint dedicated to photography, who was visiting from New York, found it heartening to see the manner in which photography was integrated into the event. “...Whether in the discussion on photobooks, which I was a panellist on, or the exhibition at the Avtar Foundation for the Arts organised by Chennai Photo Biennale Foundation in collaboration with World Wildlife Fund India—these show that the event is open to building wider communities for the medium,” he says. The two elements that further add to the popularity of Contemporary Now are that events are free to access and that the exhibitions are on display for nearly three weeks, unlike art fairs that are ticketed and have a shorter duration.

“Contemporary Now is location-agnostic, so it can go wherever there is potential” reveals Rajagopalan. “While Chennai is the origin story and our core strength, we can take the model to other cities.”
